These six evolving consciousnesses take the physical body as their co-existent support. Now, when one reflects with discernment, it can be said that the supported is the support,
because the meaning of "support" is pervasive.
There are those that have a support but are not themselves supports, because the meaning of "support" is restricted.
This being so, how many consciousnesses possess such a simultaneous support?
Treatise:
From these five consciousnesses up to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
Commentary states:
The detailed explanation of the bases according to their number consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the bases of consciousness;
second, the explanation of the mental factors (*caitta*). Within the first part, there are four further sections.
First, the interpretation of the five consciousnesses;
second, the interpretation of the sixth consciousness;
third, the interpretation of the seventh consciousness.
The fourth explanation concerns the eighth [consciousness].
This is the first [point]: the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, have four bases, namely, the five material sense organs and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
Taking the five faculties as their basis—

as in the *Mahāśāstra* (Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya) and the first chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, which state they are not one— on what scriptural authority is it recorded that the six, seven, or eight serve as their bases?
There is also explicit scriptural evidence,
such as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter seventy-six and others,
which states that when the five consciousnesses arise, there must necessarily be a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As previously cited in enumeration,
although they may differ in their objects,
[consciousness] arises only through the six [bases].
This is also because it has the same object of cognition as hearing sounds and so forth within meditative concentration; thus,
one does not perceive a time when consciousness is absent.
The five consciousnesses arise independently when hearing the text;
thus, the fourth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states that the five consciousnesses take the mind (*manas*) as their support,
because when the mind is distracted, the five do not arise.

According to that, it clarifies that five [consciousnesses] take six as their support; how then is it known that they also take seven as their support? As stated in the first chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* in the section proving the existence of the seventh consciousness:
This means that if one does not assert the existence of the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas),
the meaning would not be consistent with [the scriptures] and so forth;
this is what is intended here.
Because the seventh consciousness is defiled,
meritorious dharmas such as giving do not become untainted (anāsrava);
for they are tainted by that defiled consciousness.
As it is said in the cited verse:
"In this way, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) is the support of consciousness."
"One who has not yet extinguished the bonds of consciousness will ultimately never attain liberation," and so forth. The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* by Vasubandhu, Volume One, states:
"This does not occur within the single lifetime of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
To be free from this grasping at a self is consistent with correct reasoning;
therefore, one should know that while the five consciousnesses function as outflows,
the seventh consciousness persists until it is ultimately extinguished.
It ultimately does not become untainted (*anāsrava*), as explained in the later fascicle.

Therefore, the five consciousnesses are tainted (*sāsrava*). How is it known that they also rely upon the eighth [consciousness]? In the first chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, within the section on the "five common characteristics" (*pañca-sādharmya*).
Just as those five groups of consciousness have the five sense-faculties as their simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and the ālayavijñāna as [their] simultaneous support,
so it is here as well:
the afflicted manas has the ālayavijñāna as its simultaneous support, and so forth.

One need not trouble oneself to cite [the source], for the *Pañcaskandhaka-bhāṣya* states regarding the five common characteristics: "Although the ālayavijñāna is the co-emergent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the mental consciousness, it should not be established as its specific support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*)."
Because they share a common basis and because they are of the nature of causes and conditions,
actualization is the common basis.

The seed is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* also state that because of the existence of the ālayavijñāna, one appropriates the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), and the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) evolve based upon it. Furthermore, the first chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* explains the ālayavijñāna.
The clouds act as the causal basis for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This passage also proves that [the ālayavijñāna] serves as the support for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Below, this point is cited more than once.
Thus we know that the five consciousnesses take the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as their common support (*sādhāraṇa-āśraya*).
Although the text mentions four [supports], this is consistent with other treatises.
Why, then, must the five consciousnesses necessarily possess all four?
Treatise:
Because even if one [of the conditions] is lacking, up to the point where the basis (*āśraya*) differs.
Commentary says:
Since those five consciousnesses are considered to possess power, they fulfill the aforementioned four criteria;
therefore, among these four, if even one is lacking, [it does not constitute a sense-faculty].
Because the five consciousnesses necessarily do not arise [without them], what is the distinction between these four?
The five sense organs serve as the *sabhāga-āśraya* (co-present support) for the five consciousnesses because they apprehend the present object together;
the others are not so determined.
It alone receives this name.
The sixth consciousness serves as the *viniścaya-āśraya* (basis for discernment) for the first five consciousnesses,
because it discerns objects by sharing the same objective referent (*ālambana*) as its basis.
Although the five [sense-consciousnesses] are without conceptualization, the mind (manas) is the basis for conceptualization; thus, it is without conceptualization [in that sense].
As stated in the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra*, there are minds with conceptualization and minds without conceptualization.
It should be said that they take the same present object as their cognitive domain (*ālambana*),
and so forth, up to "due to three causes," even though there are cases where they do not take the same object, such as hearing sounds while in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
This is stated in terms of what occurs most frequently and for the longest duration;
therefore, it is called the "basis of conceptualization.
This refers to the state of non-concentration (the distracted state), not the concentrated mind. Alternatively, the term "conceptualization" does not refer to the distracted mind.
The wisdom that takes phenomena as its object within subsequently attained wisdom is also called "conceptualization," because it belongs to that same category; thus,
there is no fault of non-pervasiveness.
The mind within meditative concentration is also called "discrimination";
therefore, only the sixth consciousness receives this name.
The seventh consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses serve as the basis for defilement and purity.
The five consciousnesses become contaminated (*sāsrava*) because of this fundamental defilement;
they become uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) because of fundamental purity.
Once they have become entirely pure, the five consciousnesses do not leak.
It is named "fundamental purity" because when the sixth consciousness arises as a wholesome mind within the causal stage, it does not leak through the five sensory consciousnesses;
however, it leaks through the seventh consciousness at all times.

This is because even the wholesome mind of the mental consciousness (the sixth) is subject to leakage by that [seventh consciousness]. Furthermore, this eighth consciousness serves as the fundamental support for the first five consciousnesses.
Because it has been explained as before, these four reliances differ in their meaning. If that is so, why does the *Abhidharma* (First Chapter, etc. state:
"Visual consciousness depends on the eye and, with respect to visible forms, cognizes them as resembling visible forms"?
...and so forth, as explained at length in the treatise.
This is because the Noble Teaching speaks only of that which is proximate and concordant.
The commentary states:
The reason they are called the five faculties is because they are unique (asādhāraṇa).
First, because other consciousnesses do not rely upon it;
second, because this [consciousness] must share the same object as the five sensory consciousnesses;
and third, because it is proximate to them.
Third, because it is remote from the remaining basis (*upadhi*). Furthermore, these characteristics are concordant,
as their respective objects are distinct.

Because the sixth consciousness necessarily ceases to function [in those states].

The citations are as previously stated;
the text is easily understood.

It is said that because the ālayavijñāna exists, there is manas;
with manas as its support, the manovijñāna is able to function, and so forth.
This is as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding their shared basis, and other such passages.

Question: Since the five [sensory consciousnesses] must necessarily be accompanied by the mental faculty (manas), and the five take the mind as their support, it follows that the mind perceives the five;
therefore, the five should also be the support for the mind.
To resolve this objection, the treatise states:
"Although the five consciousnesses coexist [with them], they are not their supports."
The commentary states:
Although the mental consciousness accompanying the five sensory consciousnesses is clear and distinct,
it is not necessarily present.
Since the mental consciousness also exists at times when the five sensory consciousnesses are absent,
it is not mentioned here;
nor is it taken as the support [of the mental consciousness].
However, according to the meaning,
why is it that in other places, such as the second chapter of the Abhidharma and elsewhere,
it is stated that there are two bases for the mind?
First, the mind that has ceased without interval is the support for the subsequent life.
Second, there is the simultaneous support.
That is to say, the seventh [consciousness] does not mention the eighth.
The treatise states that the sacred teachings speak only of those that are proximate and mutually concordant.
The commentary states:
Because it is the basis for both defilement and purity,
it is as previously described.
First, they are both subsumed under the category of evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Second, they are proximate. Third, regarding their mutual conformity:
it is largely due to the seventh consciousness that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is induced to give rise to defiled attachments and the like.
Therefore, it is said that they accord with one another because both involve conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
this is not like the eighth [consciousness]. (4)
Therefore, the eighth place of existence is not mentioned;
this concludes the third section of the treatise.
"Because the seventh consciousness does not function until one reaches meditative absorption.
The commentary states:
This refers to the eighth [consciousness].
As stated in the sixty-third [treatise], the seventh is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
this is exactly the same here.
For if the eighth does not exist, the seventh also cannot exist.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) exists, there exist the manas and so forth.
Furthermore, Asvabhāva states that the fundamental consciousness is the common support (*sādhāraṇāśraya*).
Thus, one should know this [manas] as its support.
Treatise:
As stated in a verse of the Gāthā: "Up until the arising of other evolving consciousnesses.
Commentary: [As follows].
From the verses in the "Chapter on the Summary" (Saṃgrahaparivarta), the ninth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
the old verse says: "Depending upon the ālayavijñāna,
it is able to produce the evolving consciousnesses."
Depending upon the mind (manas),
the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) are able to arise;
this is slightly different from that [previous case].
Based on the preceding, relying on the *Pāda* [of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*] serves as a superior proof.
The present text can now be understood.
Treatise:
"Because the ālayavijñāna does not cease until [the state of] meditative concentration is attained. Commentary:
The fourth section below consists of four parts.
First, the statement of the thesis;
second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
third, the reconciliation of contradictions.
Regarding the four types of liberation,
the eighth [consciousness] has only one kind of basis,
namely, the seventh consciousness.
Seventh, because if it did not exist, the eight [limbs] would not function.
How is this known? The treatise states:
The treatise states that at this point, the ālayavijñāna is precisely the manas.
The commentary says:
what follows is a citation of scriptural proof.
The sixty-third [verse] states that it always functions simultaneously with the manas; furthermore, it is said that the ālayavijñāna always relies upon the defiled [manas].
This is just as it is stated in the third fascicle of the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā*: "Some say..."
The mind that is constantly associated with the four afflictions is called the "basis of defilement.
This is as Vasubandhu has stated.
Since it is thus said to be constantly based on defilement, [it follows that...]

Thus, it is known that the eighth [consciousness] takes the seven as its support. The first of the three preceding masters likewise takes the seven as the support for the eighth. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is:
because this has the nature of consciousness, it possesses a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
Alternatively, it should be based on the uninterrupted consciousness,
because the substance of that consciousness is uninterrupted;
as in the case of the seventh [consciousness], this eighth [consciousness] likewise possesses a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
As established by the aforementioned masters,
among these various explanations, the third and fourth state that the eighth consciousness relies upon the seventh;
all of these [positions] maintain that the seventh consciousness exists during the three states.
The first master cited above raised an objection, using "non-existence" as an example alongside the seven [categories].
He stated that because [the mind] is constantly continuous,
that which lacks a basis (*anāśraya*) is likewise of this same nature.
The second master asserts that only the eighth consciousness is not permitted as having a basis;
that is, in these three states, there is no seventh consciousness.
He also maintains this interpretation because it is not contradictory.
The previous second master and others asked:
"Since the eighth consciousness already has a support, namely the seventh,
why is it said that in the three states there is no seventh?"
Since the meaning [of the term] is not fixed according to its basis,
the treatise states that these three stages should also be understood in this way.
The commentary states:
This resolves the contradiction below.
The Master of the Treatise replies:
This is said in reference to the "obscured" (nivṛta) state, meaning that it is absent in three stages.
It is taught as being obscured in the sense that it constitutes an obstacle for whichever vehicle one follows.
Because it is not obscured [in those stages], it is said that the manas is absent; this does not mean that its substantial entity (svabhāva) is non-existent.
This is because the consciousness of that vehicle,
or even uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*), can also be obtained without obstruction.
Just as in the fifty-one words [of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*], although the four stages lack the term "ālayavijñāna," it is not that the substance of the eighth consciousness does not exist;
this case should be understood in the same way.
It is not that the seventh consciousness lacks a substantial entity;
because it is never interrupted, it can serve as a support. Regarding the "three stages," this is explained in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and other texts.
This refers to the four states that lack the ālayavijñāna: the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and when the noble path (āryamārga) is manifest.
These are found in the fifty-first [verse] and in the four statements of the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (17), and so forth.
The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are established as being distinct from the *ālaya*.
This refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas who have not entered the state of mindlessness (*acittaka-avasthā*).
In this regard, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses take [the ālaya] as their support.
It is not the case that when the seven do not function, the six do not function;
rather, the eight serves as the basis for the seven.
Since the seven already function, the eight should also function.
Furthermore, the eight serve as the seven supports;
when the supports shift, the seven also shift.
Thus, the eight and the seven act as mutual supports.
The transformation of the support also entails transformation;
one should apply diligent effort toward this meaning.
Herein, "transformation" refers to:
This refers to the transformation into the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, because they each have their own distinct basis,
the eighth [consciousness] of the form realm likewise relies upon the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya).
Since this is the universal basis,
why is it not mentioned? [The] Treatise [says]:
Although it belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is not included among those that serve as a basis (*āśraya*).
The commentary states:
because it lacks one essential factor, it can only function as a basis.
It is not the basis [of consciousness],
nor does it contradict the treatises.
The third master says:
The seeds of the various consciousnesses must have a basis;
the seven and eighth manifesting consciousnesses possess these three characteristics,
as explained by the preceding reasoning.
Treatise:
Consciousness-seeds cannot reach [their destination] because they lack a basis. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
This explains the seeds of the lower [level].
That seed-consciousness cannot take as its immediate object a境 (viṣaya) that is its own direct, manifest activity.
As previously stated in the established thesis: "Causing the mind and mental factors to grasp their respective objects" is the meaning of "basis" (āśraya).
The seeds are not the mind or mental factors, because they lack one of these two meanings;

thus, while they may be supported by something, they are not themselves subsumed under the category of that which possesses support. Furthermore, another interpretation of this passage holds that the manifest [mental states] do not take the seeds as their support.
The absence of the sense-object excludes it from being the support for the manifest [consciousness]. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:
first, to distinguish the active eighth consciousness from being the support for the seeds;

second, to distinguish the seeds themselves from being the support for the manifest. Although these various interpretations differ in their phrasing, they are logically sound and established by the treatise.
That which perfectly accords with the middle [teaching] is the fourth exposition. The treatise states:
"The mental factors depend upon the mind up to their association with it."
The commentary states:
The second section explains the mental factors (*caitta*).
The phenomena of the mental factors should be explained in accordance with their corresponding consciousnesses.
Initially there are four [bases], down to one;
furthermore, each is augmented by its own associated mind, which is the associated support (*samanvāgata-āśraya*).
Thus, for the first five consciousnesses, there are five types of mental factors as their supports.
Up to the eighth mind, there are two bases.
These three former masters all explain the number of bases according to the bases they themselves have established for consciousness,
and each further adds the basis of its own associated [mental factors].
Treatise:
Such an exposition perfectly accords with both reason and scripture.
Commentary states:
Third, the correct summary;
fourth, the exposition that perfectly accords with reason and scripture,
as previously cited.
Although these principles exist within various treatises,
the learned should not fail to investigate them, as they are scattered and obscured by the wording;
I shall now clarify those meanings, like a nocturnal luminary.
